 Lawmakers demand answers after leaders of USS South Dakota relieved of command
 Cmdr. Daniel Goodwin, commanding officer of USS South Dakota, shown here in June 2026. (John Narewski/U.S. Navy)
 FROM STAFF AND WIRE REPORTS
 Published 21 hours ago  · 
 Democratic lawmakers are asking for answers from the Navy after the leadership triad of USS South Dakota was relieved of duty in October.
 The decision to remove the command team came shortly after an “immediate navigational hazard” during an incident in September when the Virginia-class attack submarine descended toward shallow water, according to the The Day .
 On Thursday, U.S. Reps. Joe Courtney, D-Conn., and Adam Smith, D-Wash., sent a letter to Hung Cao, the acting secretary of the Navy, and Adm. Daryl Caudle, the Chief of Naval Operations. Courtney is the ranking member of the subcommittee on seapower and projection forces; Smith is the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee.
 “We write to express deep frustration over the Navy’s failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee of the relief of the Commanding Officer, Executive Officer, and Chief of the Boat of the USS South Dakota (SSN 790) on October 14, 2026,” the letter said.
 On Tuesday, the public affairs office for Commander, Submarine Force Atlantic confirmed that Cmdr. Daniel Goodwin was relieved of duty, citing a “loss of confidence in his ability to fulfill his assigned duties.” Lt. Cmdr. Jacqueline Penichet and Senior Chief Information Systems Technician (Submarines) Jon Nogaj also were relieved of their duties, according to Military Times .
 It was not immediately clear if the navigational hazard is the incident that resulted in the firings.
 “The Department of the Navy’s failure to communicate these incidents to Congress is unacceptable,” the lawmakers wrote. “The committee and department maintain long-standing customs for information sharing, that though not expressly written in statute, have included notifications for various types of at-sea incidents, accidents and dismissals of members of the command triad.”
 The congressmen demanded answers about the circumstances of the dismissals and clarification on whether the South Dakota encountered a “grounding or other mishap at sea.” Courtney and Smith have set a deadline of Nov. 20 for the Navy to respond.
 “The Navy’s lack of transparency leave many outstanding questions about not only what occurred, but the impact of the events leading the triad’s dismissal on the structural health of South Dakota, the well-being of the crew, and whether the incident laid bare any systemic issues with training to standard procedures that must be addressed,” the letter said.
 According to The Day, a crew member received a Navy and Marine Corps Commendation on Oct. 6. The family of Electronics Technician Navigation Seaman Ben Boyce shared the information about the incident in a Facebook post on Oct. 23, the day after the South Dakota returned to its Groton, Conn., homeport.
 The certification, which is signed by Capt. Thomas Flaherty, the commodore of Submarine Squadron 4, states that while serving as a fathometer operator onboard South Dakota in September, Boyce “recognized the rate of shoaling water presented an immediate navigational hazard to the ship and, without hesitation, called away a yellow sounding before the prescribed tripwire was reached.”
 “His superior trend analysis, sound judgment and decisive action provided the watch team the critical reaction time necessary to take action to keep the ship safe,” the certification reads.
 In a post to friends and family that included a photo of the certification, Nora Boyce-Haddow wrote that the “potential navigation hazard involving shallow water” was “the bottom of the ocean.”
 Contributing: The Day (New London, Conn.); Tribune News Service
